title: Drawing the Map: Three Strands and the Living Doughnut
reflection: Once a day, look at one person or yourself and ask only: which strand is loud today, the holding, the moving or the still? You are learning to see which way the weave has leaned, without grading anyone.

questions.q: What are the three things the group notices in a single natural breath, and what are they called in the framework?
o: A shape, a rhythm and a stillness that holds them: tamas, rajas and sattva, the three strands.
A sound, a smell and a touch that come with it: the three senses through which the breath is known.
A beginning, a middle and an end that every breath has: the three stages of a single breath.
A thought, a feeling and a wish that rise with it: the three parts of the mind at work in the breath.
questions.e: The breath has a form, a swing between two poles with a tempo, and a quiet centre that lets the shape and rhythm hold. Swamiji draws them as simple number patterns: a six-point loop of doubling, a back-and-forth of three and six, and the still nine.
questions.c: Shape, rhythm and stillness in one breath

questions.q: James has heard tamas used as an insult. What does Swamiji say it simply means?
o: Persistence, density and structure: the power to hold a form, which is what keeps a bone a bone.
Laziness and dullness, which is what the word has always meant and which a person must overcome.
Darkness of mind, which comes from a long habit of wrong action and is put right only by effort.
Pride in one’s own shape, which makes a person unwilling to change and is the cause of suffering.
questions.e: That translation has done real damage. Tamas is what keeps a cell’s wall intact and the chair a chair one second from now. It becomes a problem only when it crowds out the other two, when holding firm hardens into can’t move.
questions.c: Tamas is the power to hold a form

questions.q: “Rajas is simply dynamism, the strand that moves the structure, and it troubles us only when it overruns the structure meant to hold it.”
questions.e: Without rajas the chair holds its shape but nothing happens, and the body has form but no metabolism. A heart that stops oscillating is a dead heart: the rhythm is the life. It becomes can’t-stop only when it outruns what is meant to hold it.
questions.c: Rajas is dynamism, not a fault

questions.q: A physician sees a heart that is neither rigidly metronomic nor erratic but steadily, coherently variable. Which strand does this show?
o: Sattva: the still centre made flesh, holding form and rhythm in one coherent whole.
Tamas alone: the form is held so firmly that the heart is never allowed to change its beat.
Rajas alone: the rhythm is so lively that it is the only thing that can be seen in the heart.
None of the three, since the strands belong to the mind and are not found in the body.
questions.e: Nine is equilibrium: the eye of a hurricane, a balanced top, the hub of a galaxy, and the awareness that watched the breath. In the clinic it is cardiac coherence, a measurable poise. The old name for it is sattva, the nearest the manifest comes to the witness.
questions.c: Cardiac coherence is the still centre in the body

questions.q: Sarah takes one slow breath before she loses her temper and had thought it only a distraction. What does Swamiji say it is?
o: Far more: she takes hold of rhythm, the strand she can reach, and uses it to shift the other two.
A distraction after all, since it works only by taking her mind off the cause of the anger.
A way to hide the anger, which it does not change but only holds back for a short time.
A matter of luck, since no one can say why breathing should have any effect on the temper.
questions.e: You cannot will your cells to restructure or grab stillness by reaching for it, but you can change your breath in the next ten seconds. Rhythm is the doorway and the breath the handle. It only opens the door; the deeper work of attention and discernment waits beyond.
questions.c: Rhythm is the strand you can take hold of

questions.q: “The doughnut shape is the only shape in nature, and everything that exists is a torus.”
questions.e: Swamiji is careful not to oversell. There are spheres, spirals and branching trees, each with its own logic. The torus is one deep, recurring shape of self-sustaining life, and it is the one the three strands draw when they stand up off the page.
questions.c: The torus is one shape, not the only one

questions.q: What is wrong with ranking the strands as grades: tamas bad, rajas middling, sattva good?
o: All three are indispensable: health is the right weave, and the question is which is out of proportion.
Nothing is wrong, since the ranking is a useful guide that the old texts themselves give to each seeker.
The order is wrong: the texts really place rajas first, since movement matters most in a living thing.
Only tamas is wrong to rank, since the other two are alike and neither is better than the other.
questions.e: Escape the form strand and you would have no skeleton, a puddle; escape rhythm and you would be a corpse; stillness alone with no form or rhythm is an empty axis spinning round nothing. The clinical question is never which strand is good but which is out of proportion now.

questions.q: Sarah’s nephew cannot stop: a phone every two minutes, four hours of sleep, finishing nothing. How does Swamiji read it?
o: Rajasic drift: the rhythm has outrun the form’s ability to hold it, which is not a moral failing.
Tamasic drift: the form has grown heavy and stuck, so he needs a firmer and more regular routine.
A true sattvic state, since a person with so much energy must have a good deal of clarity as well.
A fault of character, which he can mend if his family speak to him firmly enough about it.
questions.e: The weave is pulled out of proportion, and naming the direction tells you which way to restore it. Its names in the clinic are anxiety, panic and burnout. The opposite, in someone who has not left bed for three days, is tamasic drift.
questions.c: Name which way the weave has leaned

questions.q: A man meditates daily, but his friendships have lapsed and he shares no meals with anyone. What does Swamiji say of him?
o: Not true stillness: the heavy strand in contemplative clothes; real stillness makes one more available.
A deep stillness, since a person who needs no company has reached a high state of sattva.
A fault of the practice itself, which should be given up, since it has cut him off from other people.
A man who is lazy about friends, who should be told so plainly that he must make more effort.
questions.e: Genuine equilibrium integrates your life, so a person growing in real stillness becomes warmer and more present, not less. The fault is not in the practice but in using the idea of stillness as a place to hide. Real practice ripens into presence.
questions.c: Real stillness makes a person more available

questions.q: James finds a class gone inert and heavy, and another bouncing off the walls. What does Swamiji suggest?
o: Add the missing strand: a little movement for the inert room, a slow shared breath for the wild one.
Push harder in each, since a firm hand is what any class needs to bring it back into line.
Treat both the same way, with a long pause for silence, since quiet is what every class needs.
Leave both alone, since a class that is in a certain state will not change by anything he does.
questions.e: He reads the room as too heavy or too fast and adds the missing strand. It is a better instinct than pushing harder, and less tiring. Watch what the right strand, added in the right place, does.
questions.c: Read the room, then add the missing strand
